implementation_notes: Rails receivers can let the database arbitrate: a unique index on the idempotency key plus `find_or_create_by!` (or a plain INSERT) inside the same transaction as the business writes makes ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique the duplicate signal. `find_or_create_by` alone is check-then-act unless the unique index backs it - the index, not the finder, is the claim. Outside Rails the same shape is a UNIQUE column and an INSERT OR IGNORE whose zero-change result is the duplicate.
code_sketch:
begin
  Order.transaction do
    SeenKey.find_or_create_by!(key: msg.idempotency_key)  # UNIQUE index backs this
    Order.create_from(msg)                                # same transaction
  end
rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
  ack(msg)                                                # duplicate: absorb
end
pitfalls: find_or_create_by without a unique index is a check-then-act race under concurrent consumers; the index is what makes it correct.
Rescuing RecordNotUnique around the whole transaction also swallows a uniqueness collision from business tables - keep the rescue scoped to the claim.
SeenKey rows must be pruned by age; Rails gives no automatic retention.

variants.name: In-process Set#add? guard (single process)
variants.implementation_notes: `Set#add?` returns self when the element was added and nil when it was already present, which makes the check-and-claim a single call - but MRI's GVL only makes it atomic within one process, and Rails deployments normally run several workers or threads. Use it as a fast pre-filter at most; the durable claim is the unique-index variant. Redis `SET ... NX` via redis-rb gives the same one-call claim across processes.
variants.code_sketch:
require 'set'
SEEN = Set.new

def claim(key)
  !SEEN.add?(key).nil?   # nil => already claimed
end
pitfalls: The set is per-process: Puma workers, background job processes and restarts each start with an empty guard.
Set#add? is atomic only because of the GVL; a future without it (or JRuby/TruffleRuby) changes the guarantee.
